Chapter 10

The schema: what a column is, and what a function promises

Three tables, a function table, and the parameter type that exists solely to make one error message lead somewhere.

By the end of this chapter

Write the single source of truth that the checker, the planner, completion and the documentation all read.

Everything the language knows about the world is in one file. A column has a name, a type, and a sentence; a function has parameters, a return type and a sentence. Four consumers read it and none of them has its own copy.

bag: true marks a column you can path into — attributes.http.status — and common: true marks the handful worth putting at the top of a completion list. Both are metadata *for other code*, which is the whole point of a schema.

Functions, and a return type that depends on its argument

returnsArg is the mechanism that keeps units alive through an aggregation. min(duration) is a duration and min(value) is a number; without this the aggregate would have to return dynamic, and every unit check downstream of a summarize would be lost — which is exactly where people compare a p95 against a threshold.

The parameter type that exists for one message

There is a ParamType called numeric that is neither number nor any, and it exists entirely so that one error message leads somewhere useful.

The checker’s job is to produce the message that leads somewhere

any would let percentile(service, 95) through — it runs, sorts strings, and returns a service name where a latency belongs. number would reject it and say "needs a number", which sends somebody towards toint(service) rather than towards realising the question is wrong. numeric rejects it and says the argument has to be something you can take a percentile *of*.

Checkpoint

  • You have three tables and a function list in one file.
  • You can explain what returnsArg preserves and where it would otherwise be lost.
  • You can say why numeric is not the same as number or any.
